featuredSnippet.title: What is Food Cost Percentage?

The standard formula is: Food Cost % = (Cost of Goods Sold / Food Sales) × 100. For most restaurants, a healthy benchmark is between 28% and 32%.

featureDeepDives.title: The Period Food Cost Percentage Formula & Equation
featureDeepDives.description: Period food cost measures your overall Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) relative to food revenue over a week, month, or accounting cycle. It reflects real pantry consumption including spillage, prep waste, and shrinkage.
bullets: Formula: Food Cost % = [(Beginning Inventory + Purchases - Ending Inventory) / Total Food Sales] × 100
Beginning Inventory ($): Total dollar value of food stock on hand at the start of your count period
Purchases ($): Total food and beverage vendor invoices received during the accounting cycle
Ending Inventory ($): Physical stock value remaining on shelves and in walk-ins at period close
Cost of Goods Sold (COGS): Beginning Inventory + Purchases - Ending Inventory

featureDeepDives.title: Dish & Plate-Level Recipe Costing Formula
featureDeepDives.description: To price individual menu items profitably, you must calculate the exact cost of every ingredient on the plate (proteins, sides, sauces, garnishes, seasonings, and cooking oil).
bullets: Formula: Dish Food Cost % = (Total Raw Recipe Cost / Menu Selling Price) × 100
Ideal Price Formula: Menu Price = Raw Recipe Cost / Target Food Cost % (e.g., $4.50 / 0.28 = $16.07)
Contribution Margin ($): Menu Selling Price - Total Raw Recipe Cost (gross cash generated per dish)
Target margin: Aim for 24% to 30% on core entrees to maintain healthy restaurant profitability
Use high-margin appetizers, desserts, and craft beverages (12% - 18%) to balance prime meat cuts

featureDeepDives.title: Quick Service Restaurant (QSR) & Industry Benchmark Source
featureDeepDives.description: Food cost targets vary significantly based on dining model, prep labor complexity, and ticket volume. Quick Service Restaurants (QSR) maintain lower food cost percentages due to high volume and strict portion controls.
bullets: Quick-Service Restaurant (QSR) / Fast Food: 25% – 28% (Standardized portions, bulk buying power)
Fast Casual Concepts: 26% – 30% (Fresh scratch ingredients with fast turnaround)
Full-Service Casual Dining: 28% – 32% (Diverse menu, scratch cooking, higher garnish variance)
Fine Dining & Steakhouses: 30% – 35% (Premium dry-aged beef, fresh seafood, complex plating)
Pizzerias & Italian Trattorias: 18% – 24% (Low-cost flour, grain, and tomato bases)
Coffee Shops, Cafes & Bakeries: 16% – 22% (High-markup espresso beans, teas, and baked pastries)

featureDeepDives.title: 7 Strategies for Food Cost Percentage Reduction
featureDeepDives.description: A 2% to 4% reduction in food cost percentage flows directly into bottom-line net profit. Here is how high-efficiency operators systematically reduce food costs:
bullets: Calibrate Portion Controls: Implement dedicated portion scales, color-coded ladles, and precise recipe specs

Monitor POS Recipe Depletion: Sync POS sales to inventory in real time to instantly detect shrinkage

faqs.question: What is food cost percentage?
faqs.answer: Food cost percentage is a vital restaurant financial ratio that measures the cost of food ingredients consumed relative to the gross sales generated by those items. The standard formula is: Food Cost % = (Cost of Goods Sold / Food Sales) × 100. A lower food cost percentage means a higher gross profit margin for your restaurant.

faqs.question: What is the formula for calculating food cost percentage?
faqs.answer: The period food cost percentage formula is: Food Cost % = [(Beginning Inventory + Purchases - Ending Inventory) / Total Food Sales] × 100. For an individual plate or recipe, the equation is: Dish Food Cost % = (Raw Recipe Cost / Menu Selling Price) × 100.

faqs.question: How is food cost percentage calculated step by step?
faqs.answer: To calculate food cost percentage: 1) Record your Beginning Inventory monetary value. 2) Add all new Food Purchases during the period. 3) Subtract your Ending Inventory physical count value to determine Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). 4) Divide COGS by your Total Food Sales for that period. 5) Multiply by 100 to get your Food Cost Percentage.

faqs.question: What is considered a good food cost percentage for a restaurant?
faqs.answer: For most full-service restaurants, a healthy food cost percentage ranges between 28% and 32%. Quick Service Restaurants (QSR) typically target 25% to 28%, pizzerias target 18% to 24%, and fine dining steakhouses usually run between 30% and 35% due to expensive prime proteins.

faqs.question: What is the food cost percentage benchmark for Quick Service Restaurants (QSR)?
faqs.answer: The industry benchmark for Quick Service Restaurants (QSR) is 25% to 28%. QSRs achieve this tighter margin through high order volumes, standardized supplier contracts, strict portion controls, and streamlined prep workflows.

faqs.question: What percentage should food cost and operating costs be in a restaurant?
faqs.answer: In a well-managed restaurant, Food & Beverage costs should represent 28% to 32% of sales, and Labor costs should be 28% to 32%. Combined, these represent Prime Cost, which should remain below 60% to 62%. Occupancy/Rent should be 6% to 10%, Direct Operating Expenses 12% to 18%, leaving a Net Profit Margin of 5% to 15%.

faqs.question: How can a restaurant achieve food cost percentage reduction?
faqs.answer: Restaurants can reduce food cost percentage by: 1) Calibrating portion control with scales and recipe cards. 2) Logging daily kitchen waste and spoilage. 3) Performing weekly inventory counts on high-cost proteins. 4) Negotiating bulk purchase prices with suppliers. 5) Cross-utilizing ingredients across multiple menu items. 6) Using automated POS and inventory management software like SavoryOps to catch inventory shrinkage in real time.

faqs.question: What is the difference between ideal food cost and actual food cost?
faqs.answer: Ideal (theoretical) food cost is what your ingredient cost should have been based purely on recipes and POS sales volume. Actual food cost is what you physically spent based on beginning inventory, purchases, and ending stock counts. The difference between the two is known as Food Cost Variance, which highlights kitchen waste, over-portioning, spoilage, or theft.

faqs.question: What is a KOT (Kitchen Order Ticket) in a restaurant?
faqs.answer: A Kitchen Order Ticket (KOT) is an operational document generated when an order is placed in a restaurant. It contains the table number, items ordered, quantity, preparation modifiers, and server name. It informs kitchen chefs what to prepare, in what sequence, and for which table.

faqs.question: What is the difference between KOT and BOT?
faqs.answer: KOT stands for Kitchen Order Ticket (routed to food preparation stations like the grill, fryer, or bakery), while BOT stands for Bar Order Ticket (routed specifically to the bartender for alcoholic beverages, mocktails, and specialty coffee drinks).

faqs.question: What is a Void KOT and why is it important?
faqs.answer: A Void KOT occurs when an item or entire ticket is cancelled after being sent to the kitchen. SavoryOps tracks Void KOTs with mandatory manager PIN authorization and reason codes, preventing food waste, employee theft, and revenue leakage.

faqs.question: Can SavoryOps print physical KOTs and also show digital kitchen screens?
faqs.answer: Yes. SavoryOps supports a hybrid workflow. You can print physical thermal KOTs at the kitchen pass while simultaneously displaying the digital orders on interactive kitchen display (KDS) tablets.

faqs.question: How does SavoryOps smart KOT prevent billing mistakes?
faqs.answer: Every generated KOT is permanently linked to the specific table session. When the guest requests the final bill, all items from multiple KOTs are automatically consolidated into one final invoice with zero missing items.

faqs.question: Can multiple KOTs be created for a single table?
faqs.answer: Yes. Guests often order starters first, followed by main courses and desserts later. SavoryOps allows unlimited incremental KOTs per table, keeping separate course numbers while combining them on the final receipt.
